# PanPan Marine

> PanPan Marine (operated by Guangzhou PanPanTech Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, China) supplies underwater inspection and work-class ROVs, crawler inspection robots, long-distance tunnel inspection ROVs, underwater cleaning and dredging robots, unmanned surface vessels and ocean observation equipment for dams, hydropower tunnels, intakes, sumps, ports, offshore wind and coastal waters. Equipment is manufactured by Boya Gongdao (ROBOOCEAN). Contact: panda@panpantechnology.com.

Key facts:
- Figures are manufacturer figures and are confirmed for the supplied version in each quotation.
- Case studies are manufacturer projects in China, not projects delivered by PanPan Marine.
- Quotations are itemised per project; no list prices are published.
- Export of unmanned surface vessels and some observation equipment is subject to approval per project.

## Equipment
- [R-20 / R-20Li Portable Inspection ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-20-portable-inspection-rov/): A compact 16 kg observation ROV with a tethered power supply (R-20) or an internal lithium battery (R-20Li), for fast visual checks where vehicle size and handling matter. Key figures: Vehicle weight 16 kg; Depth rating 150 m; Payload 0.6 kg; Dimensions 430 × 380 × 340 mm.
- [R-30 Inspection ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-30-inspection-rov/): A tethered inspection ROV for visual assessment of submerged structures, with payload and sensor selection matched to the task. Key figures: Vehicle weight 21 kg; Depth rating 300 m; Payload 3 kg; Dimensions 500 × 398 × 356 mm.
- [R-45 Inspection ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-45-inspection-rov/): A tethered inspection platform with a higher brochure payload than the R-30, for projects needing additional sensing or tooling. Key figures: Vehicle weight 42 kg; Depth rating 350 m; Payload 8 kg; Dimensions 675 × 500 × 445 mm.
- [R-150 Light Work-Class ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-150-light-work-class-rov/): A 195 kg light work-class ROV rated to 500 m, with a 20 kg payload and modular interfaces for sensors and tools on offshore and hydraulic-structure tasks. Key figures: Vehicle weight 195 ± 5 kg; Depth rating 500 m; Payload 20 kg; Dimensions 1,170 × 780 × 770 mm.
- [R-400 Work-Class ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-400-work-class-rov/): A 520 kg work-class ROV rated to 800 m, with a 50 kg payload and 12 thrusters for offshore wind foundations, subsea cables and hydropower tasks. Key figures: Vehicle weight 520 ± 10 kg; Depth rating 800 m; Payload 50 kg; Dimensions 2,080 × 1,020 × 1,150 mm.
- [R-2000 Heavy Work-Class ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-2000-heavy-work-class-rov/): A 2.2 t heavy work-class ROV rated to 1,000 m, supplied with a tether management system and shore control for subsea engineering, survey and recovery tasks. Key figures: Vehicle weight 2,200 kg; Depth rating 1,000 m; Payload 100 kg (without TMS); Dimensions 2,500 × 1,400 × 1,500 mm.
- [R-4000 Heavy Work-Class ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/r-4000-heavy-work-class-rov/): A 3.3 t heavy work-class ROV rated to 3,000 m with a 200 kg payload and titanium-alloy frame, for deep-water engineering maintenance and resource exploration. Key figures: Vehicle weight 3,300 kg; Depth rating 3,000 m (6,000 m custom on request); Payload 200 kg; Dimensions 3,000 × 1,700 × 1,650 mm.
- [A-30 Compact Crawler Inspection Robot](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/a-30-crawler-inspection-robot/): A 35 kg crawler inspection robot that swims, rolls onto a wall and crawls along it, for close inspection of tanks, pools, pipes and structure surfaces to 100 m. Key figures: Vehicle weight 35 kg; Depth rating 100 m; Payload 3 kgf (test method to confirm); Dimensions 400 × 400 × 300 mm.
- [A-400 Crawler Inspection Robot](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/a-400-crawler-inspection-robot/): A 400 kg tracked underwater robot that switches between swimming and crawling on submerged structures, for dam, intake and hydropower inspection to 300 m. Key figures: Vehicle weight 400 kg; Depth rating 300 m; Motion modes Free swimming + tracked crawling; Dimensions 1,800 × 1,200 × 750 mm.
- [AD-400 Tunnel Inspection ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/ad-400-tunnel-inspection-rov/): A specialist platform for long-distance inspection of flooded water tunnels, combining a tethered vehicle with project-specific sensing and tether management. Key figures: Vehicle weight 300 kg; Depth rating 1,000 m; Official-site maximum range 5 km; Dimensions 1,600 × 900 × 548 mm.
- [A-80 Underwater Cleaning Robot](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/a-80-cleaning-robot/): A floating and crawling underwater platform described by the manufacturer for contact cleaning, with cavitation water-jet and brush configurations subject to application review. Key figures: Vehicle weight 100 kg; Depth rating 300 m; Payload 15 kg; Dimensions 880 × 710 × 490 mm.
- [AD-100 Underwater Dredging Robot](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/ad-100-dredging-robot/): A remotely operated platform described in the manufacturer brochure for underwater sump dredging, with suction, conveyance and treatment selected together. Key figures: Vehicle weight 100 kg; Dimensions 815 × 620 × 690 mm; Thruster arrangement 6 (2 horizontal + 4 vertical); Cameras Front and rear.
- [USUG-Skaters Unmanned Survey Vessel](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/usug-skaters-unmanned-survey-vessel/): A 4.5 m autonomous catamaran for bathymetry, hydraulic-structure inspection and hydrological monitoring, with modular payload bays and an optional ROV and docking station. Key figures: Weight 1.1 ± 0.2 t; Draught 50 ± 10 cm; Minimum water depth 1 m; Dimensions 4.46 × 2.50 × 1.97 m.
- [S-Cleaner Surface Cleaning Vessel](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/s-cleaner-surface-cleaning-vessel/): A 2 m, 270 kg autonomous catamaran that detects and collects floating debris in harbours, reservoirs, rivers and scenic waters, using lidar and cameras to avoid obstacles. Key figures: Weight 270 ± 5 kg; Draught 50 ± 10 cm; Minimum water depth 1 m; Dimensions 2 × 1.4 × 1.4 m.
- [M-Cleaner Large Surface Cleaning Vessel](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/m-cleaner-surface-cleaning-vessel/): A 5 m-class autonomous cleaning vessel with a 500 kg debris capacity for harbours, coastal waters within 2 km of shore, lakes and reservoirs, including algae and floating waste. Key figures: Draught ≤ 80 cm; Minimum water depth 1 m; Dimensions ≤ 5 m long, ≤ 2.5 m wide; Debris capacity ≥ 500 kg.
- [USOL10 Ocean Observation Vessel](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/usol10-ocean-observation-vessel/): An 11 m unmanned observation vessel for coastal and offshore monitoring, carrying multibeam, ADCP, CTD and water samplers, with an optional two-person manual mode. Key figures: Length 11 m; Full-load displacement 8 t; Cruise speed 8 kn (4.1 m/s); Endurance 200 min at 8 kn (to confirm).
- [USTL15 Unmanned Transport Vessel](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/ustl15-unmanned-transport-vessel/): A 15 m unmanned transport vessel with at least 1,000 kg payload for offshore supply runs, equipment sea trials and area patrols. Key figures: Length 15 m; Working speed ≥ 4 m/s; Maximum speed ≥ 6 m/s; Maximum payload ≥ 1,000 kg.
- [HY-FB-GX01 Ocean Optical Buoy](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/hy-fb-gx01-ocean-optical-buoy/): A 2 m moored buoy for long-term optical, water-quality and weather observation, designed to stay level in wind and waves. Key figures: Buoy diameter 2 m; Design draught 1.25 m; Water depth 3–30 m; Design life 10 years.
- [GL-1300 Underwater Glider](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/gl-1300-underwater-glider/): A buoyancy-driven underwater glider rated beyond 1,300 m, with glide and vertical-profile modes for long-duration ocean observation. Key figures: Maximum depth ≥ 1,300 m; Modes Glide and vertical profile; Average glide speed ≥ 0.5 kn; Battery Primary lithium, ≥ 500 Ah.
- [ROV tools & accessories](https://www.panpanmarine.com/equipment/rov-tools-accessories/): manipulator arms, intervention tools, sensors, thrusters and release hooks.

## Applications
- [Industrial underwater inspection](https://www.panpanmarine.com/solutions/industrial-underwater-inspection/): Choose an ROV around the inspection result you need, then work back through visibility, access, depth and sensor requirements.
- [Long-distance underwater tunnel inspection](https://www.panpanmarine.com/solutions/underwater-tunnel-inspection/): Inspection of flooded water tunnels depends on navigation, tether control and recovery as much as the vehicle’s rated range.
- [Robotic underwater trash-rack cleaning](https://www.panpanmarine.com/solutions/underwater-trash-rack-cleaning/): Evaluate contact cleaning of submerged intake and trash-rack surfaces against the deposits, rack geometry and support equipment.
- [Robotic sump cleaning & confined-space dredging](https://www.panpanmarine.com/solutions/underwater-sump-cleaning/): For submerged sumps, a viable dredging system connects the vehicle to a pump, conveyance route and sediment-treatment plan.
- [Autonomous water-surface cleaning](https://www.panpanmarine.com/solutions/water-surface-cleaning/): Choosing a surface-cleaning vessel depends on the water area, the type and volume of debris, shore facilities for docking and charging, and whether local rules allow unmanned operation.

- [Long-distance water-tunnel inspection in China](https://www.panpanmarine.com/case-studies/long-distance-water-tunnel-inspection/): The supplied manufacturer brochure describes an AD-400 long-distance headrace water-tunnel inspection project associated with China Southern Power Grid.
- [Underwater intake trash-rack cleaning in China](https://www.panpanmarine.com/case-studies/underwater-trash-rack-cleaning/): The supplied manufacturer brochure identifies an A-80 application at the Baihetan hydropower intake trash rack in China.
- [Dual-mode crawler inspection of hydropower structures in China](https://www.panpanmarine.com/case-studies/hydropower-dam-crawler-inspection/): The supplied manufacturer brochure describes the development of a dual-mode (swimming and crawling) underwater inspection robot for China Yangtze Power, for inspection of submerged hydropower structures.
- [Autonomous surface cleaning at a fishing port in China](https://www.panpanmarine.com/case-studies/fishing-port-surface-cleaning/): The supplied manufacturer brochure describes routine surface cleaning by an S-Cleaner vessel at the Yazhou central fishing port in Sanya, China.

## Buying guides
- [Fish Farm Net and Mooring Inspection with Small ROVs](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/fish-farm-net-inspection-rov/): Small ROVs are well suited to routine visual inspection of nets, moorings and seabed around fish farms, provided they are matched to the site: thrust for the current, a tether set-up that will not snag the net, sensors for the visibility, a deployment method that fits the workboat, and cleaning procedures that meet biosecurity rules. Inspection is the starting point; net cleaning and mortality removal need different tools and should be evaluated separately with site trials.
- [How Much Floating Debris Can a Cleaning Vessel Collect in a Day?](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/floating-debris-collection-capacity/): Daily collection is limited by whichever runs out first: basket capacity multiplied by the number of unloading trips, operating hours between charges, or the amount of debris the vessel can actually reach. Rated coverage tells you how much water the vessel can sweep, not how much debris it will collect. Estimate each limit separately and confirm with a trial.
- [Autonomous Surface Cleaning Vessels for Harbours and Reservoirs: A Buyer’s Guide](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/autonomous-surface-cleaning-vessel-guide/): Start with how much floating debris arrives, what it is and how often the water must be cleared. Then choose the vessel size for the water area, plan where it will dock, charge and unload, and confirm that local rules allow unmanned operation and that its radio links can be certified. Judge the result by measured area, collected weight and operating hours over a trial period, not by the rated coverage alone.
- [Underwater Trash Rack Cleaning: Robotic Options, Risks and Acceptance Tests](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/underwater-trash-rack-cleaning-robot/): Robotic trash-rack cleaning uses a remotely operated vehicle that holds onto the rack and removes attached deposits — typically biological growth, shells or hardened sediment — with a water jet or brush. It suits deposits that fixed rakes cannot remove and situations where draining the intake or sending divers is costly or risky. It does not replace debris raking for large floating material. Survey the rack and deposit first, then agree a trial and acceptance test on a representative area.
- [Launch and Recovery for a 200–500 kg ROV: Crane, A-Frame or Davit?](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/rov-launch-and-recovery/): For vehicles of roughly 200–500 kg, a davit or a vessel crane can work in calm conditions, while an A-frame or dedicated launch and recovery system (LARS) gives better control through the splash zone and in higher sea states. The choice depends on the vessel, the sea state you need to work in, deck space and crew experience. Plan the launch and recovery system as part of the ROV purchase, not as an afterthought.
- [Subsea Cable Route and Burial-Depth Surveys: Sensors, ROV Class and Deliverables](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/subsea-cable-route-burial-survey/): Decide which question the survey must answer: is the cable visible and intact, has the seabed changed along the route, is it still buried to the required depth, or are there free spans? Visual checks need a camera; seabed change needs sonar mapping; burial depth needs a cable-tracking or magnetic method; free spans need both. Each step adds sensors, positioning requirements and often a larger ROV. Write the questions and acceptance criteria into the survey specification.
- [Observation-Class vs Work-Class ROV: The Practical Difference](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/observation-class-vs-work-class-rov/): Observation-class ROVs are small, quick to deploy and built to look: cameras plus light sensors. Work-class ROVs are larger and more powerful, built to carry heavy sensors and tools and to work in current. Between them sit light work-class vehicles. Choose the smallest class that can deliver your result in your conditions, because every step up adds deployment equipment, crew and operating cost.
- [Offshore Wind Monopile and Scour Inspection with ROVs: What to Specify](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/offshore-wind-monopile-scour-inspection/): Start from the deliverable the asset owner needs — general visual condition, scour depth and extent, cathodic-protection readings, marine-growth thickness or cable-entry condition — because each needs different sensors and a different level of ROV. An observation-class ROV can cover visual checks in good conditions; scour mapping, CP measurements and work around cable protection usually call for more payload, more thrust and better positioning. Plan the weather window, vessel and data format with the same care as the vehicle.
- [Dam Inspection: When to Use a Swimming ROV and When to Use a Crawler](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/dam-inspection-rov-vs-crawler/): Use a free-swimming ROV when you need to cover many structures quickly in calm water and a stable standoff view is enough. Use a crawler, or a robot that both swims and crawls, when you must hold position on a surface in flow or turbulence, inspect large areas systematically, or bring a camera or tool very close to the surface. The surface itself — concrete, steel, fouling, geometry — decides whether crawling is practical.
- [How Long Should an ROV Tether Be?](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/rov-tether-length/): Add the vertical depth, the horizontal distance from the launch point to the furthest target and the extra length needed for the route, then add slack so the vehicle is never pulling against a tight tether. Do not simply order the longest tether available: more length means more drag, more voltage drop and heavier handling equipment. Ask the supplier to confirm the length against your route and current.
- [Penstock and Headrace Tunnel Inspection Without Dewatering: A Planning Guide](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/tunnel-inspection-without-dewatering/): A flooded tunnel can often be inspected without draining it, but rarely without changing how it operates. Most wet inspections still need flow stopped or reduced, a safe access point, a planned tether route, a way to locate findings and an agreed recovery plan. Wet inspection is well suited to screening condition and finding defects; some measurements and repairs still need a dry tunnel. Decide what the inspection must prove before choosing the method.
- [What an ROV Depth Rating Does — and Doesn’t — Tell You](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/rov-depth-rating-explained/): A depth rating tells you the depth the vehicle’s housings are designed for. It does not tell you whether every sensor and tool is rated to the same depth, whether the tether is long enough, or whether the vehicle can work in the current and visibility at your site. Specify the working depth with a margin, then check every component and the site conditions against it.
- [How Much Payload Does an Inspection ROV Really Need?](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/inspection-rov-payload-capacity/): Size payload from the result you need, not from the largest number on a datasheet. List every sensor, tool and mounting part, convert each to its in-water weight, add margin for trim and buoyancy changes, then check that the vehicle can still hold position against current and tether drag. A brochure payload is a starting point; the supplier should confirm the integrated configuration, its trim and its power and data connections before you order.
- [Underwater Cleaning vs Dredging: Choosing the Right System](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/underwater-cleaning-vs-dredging/): Choose underwater cleaning when the required result is removing deposits from a submerged surface. Consider dredging when the task is collecting and transferring accumulated sediment. Some sites need both. Specify the material, access, required result and complete supporting system before selecting a robot: the attachment, pump, hoses, separation equipment and handling arrangements can determine whether the proposed configuration is suitable.
- [How to Choose an Industrial Inspection ROV](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/industrial-inspection-rov-selection-guide/): Choose an industrial inspection ROV by defining the evidence your inspection must produce, then checking visibility, access, depth, flow, integrated sensors and recovery. Compare the complete field system, including its tether, control station, power, training and support. Shortlist a platform only when the supplier can demonstrate the proposed configuration against your task and provide a clear, itemized quotation.
- [Flooded Tunnel Inspection: A Procurement Planning Guide](https://www.panpanmarine.com/blog/flooded-tunnel-inspection-procurement-guide/): To procure a flooded tunnel inspection system, define the inspection result first, then compare the complete vehicle, sensing, tether, power, positioning and recovery package against your actual tunnel. Require sample deliverables, a stated configuration, site assumptions and an agreed acceptance plan before comparing prices. A manufacturer's maximum range is a starting specification; it does not establish usable coverage, defect-location accuracy or recoverability in your tunnel.
